source: Del et al. (2026) How Uncertainty Estimation Scales with Sampling in Reasoning Models
finding: Gap 1 and 2. Three current reasoning models, 17 tasks, black-box only. Verbalized confidence (VC) from one run is already a decent signal. Self-consistency (SC) starts lower than VC at equal sample count. Both improve with more samples, VC mostly in math.
numbers: Models gpt-oss-20b (high effort), Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-R1-8B; up to 100 samples per question. Math AUROC: VC K=1 71.3, K=8 81.4 (+10.1); STEM +4.6 and humanities +4.1, saturating by K=5. SC at K=2: 70.5 math, 66.6 STEM, 63.3 humanities. On MMLU-Pro Math SC@2 65.9 and GSM8K 63.3 versus VC@1 78.8 and 68.7. SC does not overtake VC up to K=8.
quote: Verbalized confidence is a strong baseline that can be further improved via sampling
limits: Open-weight mid-size models only; MMLU-Pro is mostly multiple choice; AUROC not ECE; confidence asked after the answer in the same run, so it is not a before/after comparison.
agent_relevance: For a reasoning-model agent, one self-reported confidence per run is a strong first signal. Do not replace it with k-sample agreement at small k.

source: Del et al. (2026) How Uncertainty Estimation Scales with Sampling in Reasoning Models (hybrid signal and token-matched test)
finding: Gap 2 crossover. The best use of a second sample is to combine its agreement with the verbalized confidence (SCVC), not to sample more for one signal. With K=2 the hybrid beats either signal alone even at K=8. Returns diminish after that, and SC and VC become more correlated as K grows.
numbers: Math AUROC: VC@1 71.3 -> SCVC@2 84.2 (+12.9); best single signal at K=8 is 81.4 (VC) and 79.6 (SC). STEM 73.8 -> 80.2 (+6.4); humanities 68.5 -> 74.9 (+6.4). Math SCVC K=2 -> K=5 +2.7; K=5 -> K=8 about +1.5; K=2 -> K=8 +4.2 math, about +2 STEM and humanities. Matched-token test with gpt-oss-20b (low vs high reasoning) shows SC is much weaker under extended reasoning than under shallow generation, while VC stays strong.
limits: Crossover is about the combination, not VC vs SC. Domain dependent: strongest in math (the RLVR domain). One model for the token-matched test. No test on code or puzzle tasks such as ARC.
agent_relevance: Cheap rule for the schema: one run with stated confidence, plus one extra sample whose agreement is mixed into the score. A third and later sample gives much less.

source: Del et al. (2026) section 3.5: six verbalized-confidence prompts, including post-hoc judge passes
finding: Gap 1 and 9. Compared confidence stated alongside the answer (elicitation) with a second pass that reads the whole reasoning trace and then outputs confidence (judge). All used a 1-100 scale. Judge passes did not clearly win and cost another reasoning pass.
numbers: Domain-averaged AUROC (math/STEM/humanities) from Table 3: VaEl best in STEM (77.2) and 73.2 in math; verification judge VeJu 73.8 in math; EpEl 69.44/76.11/71.43; VeEl 70.80/76.95/70.61; VaJu 70.35/76.24/71.78; VeJu 73.82/76.37/71.49; EpJu 67.59/72.00/67.97 (epistemic-marker judge consistently weakest).
limits: Same three models. Only a 1-100 scale was used, so this does not answer the scale-granularity gap (gap 9). Not a clean confidence-before-reasoning test.
agent_relevance: Confidence given with the answer is about as good as a later judge pass on current reasoning models; a minimal prompt is enough. Extra self-assessment prompts are not supported.

source: Hiremath and Hiremath (2026) Calibration Drift Under Reasoning: How Chain-of-Thought Budgets Induce Overconfidence
finding: Gap 1. Claims calibration error may first fall then rise as the reasoning budget grows (hypothesis lock-in). The data are small and the 70B result is inconclusive by the authors' own statement.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.3-70B; 47 reasoning-trap questions; four budgets; three seeds; 1,368 API calls, 574 valid responses. 8B non-monotonic; 70B baseline only.
limits: Tiny question set, many invalid responses (574 of 1,368), not current reasoning models, preprint. Treat as a hypothesis, not evidence.
agent_relevance: Weak support only for a stop rule that watches confidence versus an accuracy estimate (CABStop). Do not rely on it.

source: Lacombe, Wu and Dilworth (2025) Don't Think Twice! Over-Reasoning Impairs Confidence Calibration
finding: Gap 1 and 7. On the ClimateX task (labelling the confidence level that IPCC experts attached to statements), longer reasoning budgets made models more overconfident. Retrieval of evidence beat pure reasoning by a wide margin. This is the opposite direction to the 'search tools cause overconfidence' result of Xuan et al.
numbers: Reasoning models 48.7% accuracy (kappa-type score 31.6%); non-reasoning 45.0%; search-augmented 89.3% accuracy (85.7%). Accuracy for Gemini 2.5 Flash falls as thinking budget rises and collapses beyond 256 tokens in one plot.
limits: The task is rating an expert's stated confidence on a statement, not the model's confidence in its own answer, so it is only an indirect test. Gemini-family models; workshop preprint.
agent_relevance: Longer thinking is not a free calibration gain. Retrieved evidence can help when the task is knowledge-bound.

source: Wang et al. (2026) On the Pitfalls of Verbalized Confidence Priors for Calibrating Large Reasoning Models
finding: Gap 1 and 10. Off-the-shelf reasoning models put their verbalized confidence on a few high values. Calibration training lowers ECE but AUROC often does not rise, and can fall out of domain.
numbers: Fewer than 5% of responses below 0.5 confidence; 70-90% of responses on fewer than 7 values. After RL, mean confidence on MinervaMath only 9.7% lower than on Math500 despite a 39.1% drop in Pass@1. One method: ECE falls 29.05 -> 8.83. CalibSFT over 16 benchmarks: average ECE 23.41 -> 12.49, average AUROC 70.49 -> 73.95. A baseline out of distribution: ECE 46.94 -> 25.49 while AUROC 65.71 -> 61.20. In another setting ECE fell from 23.8-25.8% to 7.8-14.2% while AUROC steadily degraded.
limits: Training-based fix (RL and SFT), not a prompt. Preprint. Shows the problem, not a scaffold remedy.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a calibration gain unless AUROC is reported too, and test out of domain. Stated confidence of reasoning models bunches at the top.

source: Yang et al. (2026) Scaling with Confidence: Calibrating Confidence of LLMs for Adaptive Test Time Scaling (C3RL and CAS)
finding: Gap 3. A stopping rule that uses calibrated verbalized confidence to decide when to stop sampling beats fixed-N majority voting in cost. It also uses less than half the samples of Adaptive-Consistency (agreement-only stopping) on text tasks.
numbers: CAS reduces inference budget up to 12.33x versus majority voting at N=64. On out-of-distribution text tasks CAS needs 5.19 samples versus 12.87 for Adaptive-Consistency to match MV(N=64) accuracy. Six benchmarks (MMLU validation, FOLIO, GSM8K plus 3 multimodal). Confidence quality depends on RL training (C3RL); an untrained base Qwen2.5VL-7B has average AUROC 0.578 and ECE 0.386.
limits: The calibrated confidence comes from an RL-trained model; prompt-only gating may not match. Benchmarks are QA, math and multimodal, not ARC grids or BrainTeaser riddles. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Supports confidence-gated stopping over fixed n in principle. Still no direct test on ARC or BrainTeaser.

source: Aghazadeh et al. (2026) CGES: Confidence-Guided Early Stopping for Efficient and Accurate Self-Consistency (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Gap 3. Bayesian early stopping from per-sample confidence cuts calls by more than half versus fixed self-consistency at equal accuracy. Beats other early-stopping baselines (ESC, ASC, DSC).
numbers: Five reasoning benchmarks, two open 7B models: average calls 16.0 -> 6.7 (58% fewer) within 0.4 percentage points of SC. Sequential sampling costs wall time because SC can batch all samples in one call.
limits: Confidence from token probabilities or a reward model, not verbalized. Needs open-weight access or a reward model. Guarantees assume directional drift of the confidence signal.
agent_relevance: Gating beats fixed n on cost for numeric/short-answer reasoning; the gate needs a usable score. A verbalized score is weaker than these signals.

source: Xuan et al. (2026) The Confidence Dichotomy: Analyzing and Mitigating Miscalibration in Tool-Use Agents
finding: Gap 7. This is the Xuan 2026 source behind claim K14, so it is the original, not a replication. Evidence tools (web search) raise overconfidence; verification tools (code interpreter on MATH-500, AIME) keep better calibration. Pilot used Qwen2.5-3B only. The authors cite Wei et al. (2025a) as agreeing that search harms calibration.
numbers: Pilot (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) MATH-500 accuracy: direct 63.4, prompting tool use 48.6, RL tool use 77.0; search conditions raise Mean Confidence on Incorrect with t-tests significant from direct prompting to RL tool use. CAR (margin-separated calibration reward), SimpleQA-verified: Qwen2.5-3B ECE 0.213 -> 0.175, AUROC 0.659 -> 0.823; Qwen2.5-7B ECE 0.204 -> 0.176, AUROC 0.831 -> 0.790; Qwen3-4B ECE 0.140 -> 0.034, AUROC 0.825 -> 0.765.
limits: Small models (3B-7B), Search-R1 setup with a local Wikipedia retriever. Not an independent replication. The per-condition pilot numbers were hard to read from the PDF text, so only the stated direction is relied on. The CAR rows again show ECE gains with flat or lower AUROC.
agent_relevance: Weak but consistent hint: tool outputs that can be checked (run code) help; noisy retrieved text does not. Verify before trusting confidence after retrieval.

source: Kumaran et al. (2025) How Overconfidence in Initial Choices and Underconfidence Under Criticism Modulate Change of Mind in LLMs (re-read for gap 4)
finding: Gap 4. The choice-supportive bias is real and depends on the answer being the model's own. When the visible earlier answer was said to come from a different LLM, the bias vanished. The paper measures change of mind and confidence, not whether the final answer is more or less accurate.
numbers: Own answer hidden vs shown: change of mind 32.5% vs 13.1%. Told the answer came from another LLM: 31.3% hidden vs 33.2% shown, no significant difference. Models: Gemma 3, GPT-4o, o1-preview. LLMs also overweight opposing advice relative to a Bayesian update.
quote: the LLM shows an irrational bias to stick with the original answer, as long as it is its own
limits: No accuracy-of-revision measure; the task is a two-option latitude question with synthetic advice, not open-ended review. So whether masking improves revise-step accuracy is not tested.
agent_relevance: Attributing the earlier answer to another reviewer removed the stickiness in this test. A cheap masking or re-attribution test for revise steps is justified, but not yet shown to raise accuracy.

source: AAAI-25 paper on memory-driven choice-supportive bias in LLM agents (found by search; page not opened)
finding: Gap 4. Search result summary only: LLM agents can show memory-driven choice-supportive bias, and the bias may remain even when contextual hallucination is reduced. I did not open the paper, so no numbers.
agent_relevance: Second source for choice-supportive bias in agents with memory. Needs reading before use.

source: Kim, Liao, Vorvoreanu, Ballard and Vaughan (2024) 'I'm Not Sure, But...': Impact of LLM Uncertainty Expression on User Reliance and Trust (FAccT)
finding: Gap 5. Pre-registered experiment, N=404, medical questions with a fictional LLM search engine. First-person hedges ('I'm not sure, but...') cut agreement with the AI and raised participant accuracy; impersonal hedges had weaker, mostly non-significant effects. Overreliance on wrong answers fell but was not removed.
numbers: Agreement with AI: Control 80.9%, Uncertain1st 74.8% (significant), UncertainGeneral 77.6% (not significant), No-AI 58.4%. Confidence in AI answer: Control 3.95, Uncertain1st 3.66 (significant), UncertainGeneral 3.80 (n.s.), 5-point scale. The correctness table lists 63.9%, 72.8% and 74.2% for different conditions; Control < Uncertain1st is significant (column labels unclear in the text extraction).
limits: Human readers, medical questions, hedge placed at random, not tied to true correctness. No AUC and no model reader. So it does not answer whether the wording transfers to a model reader.
agent_relevance: Human-facing: use first-person hedged wording for low-confidence answers. For a model reader (a later agent step) this is untested; use numeric confidence there.

source: Cacioli (2026) Do LLMs Know What They Know? Measuring Metacognitive Efficiency with Signal Detection Theory, version 3
finding: Gap 6 and a correction to c14. Version 3 re-scored answers after finding a length-biased scorer. The strong inverse link between accuracy and efficiency in v1 and v2 weakened to -0.80 on TriviaQA and 0.00 on Natural Questions. Efficiency (meta-I2r) is domain-specific: weakest in Science and Technology for all four models.
numbers: 224,000 trials, four 7-9B models. Meta-I2r varies 1.98-fold across models. Table 3 (corrected): Llama-3-Base acc 0.478, meta-I2r 0.300; Mistral-Instruct 0.560 / 0.206 (was 0.328, now third of four); Llama-3-Instruct 0.584 / 0.263; Gemma-2-Instruct 0.627 / 0.151. Gemma domain values: Science and Tech 0.079, Pop Culture 0.275. Scorer missed 53% and 26% of two models' human-correct answers (1,200 adjudications). Metacognitive information tracks the selective-prediction gain with Spearman +1.00 (n=4 models).
limits: Small open models, token log-probabilities not verbalized confidence, factual QA only, n=4 models so correlations are anecdotal. Independent author, preprint (pre-registered).
agent_relevance: No sign of one general metacognition factor across domains: the same model is weakest in science. Per-domain, per-model confidence checks are needed. Also a warning that an automatic answer scorer can change the headline result.

source: Servajean and Servajean (2026) Measuring (some aspects of) the metacognition of AI
finding: Gap 6. Applies meta-d' and M-ratio to three current LLMs on three tasks. All show some but suboptimal metacognitive sensitivity. AUC2 mixes task skill and metacognition; M-ratio can reverse the AUC2 ordering. For the same model, M-ratio is steadier across tasks than AUC2 for two of three models.
numbers: GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, Mistral-Medium-2508; tasks A, B, C. Across tasks, M-ratio of GPT-5 and DeepSeek did not differ significantly, while AUC2 differed and tracked d' (Spearman rs = 0.9, p < 0.002). Mistral's M-ratio differed between task A and the other two (differences 0.13 and 0.20). GPT-5 M-ratio higher than DeepSeek by 0.16 (task A) and 0.21 (task B). Mistral in task B had higher M-ratio but lower AUC2 than DeepSeek in task A. All M-ratios above 0.5 and below optimal.
limits: Three tasks, three models, preprint, 2-choice tasks. Partial support for stable efficiency within a model, not proof of a general factor. Rahnev (d16) shows M-ratio is noisy in humans.
agent_relevance: M-ratio is a fairer cross-task measure than AUROC for a binary task. For an agent report both; do not claim a domain-general factor yet.

source: Fleming, Weil, Nagy, Dolan and Rees (2010) Relating introspective accuracy to individual differences in brain structure (Science)
finding: Gap 8. Opened the full text. Metacognitive accuracy differs greatly between people at the same task performance, and relates to anterior prefrontal grey matter. The N=32 recalled earlier is confirmed.
numbers: 32 healthy adults; 2-interval visual discrimination with a staircase holding about 71% correct (range 70-74%); confidence on a 1-6 scale. Type-2 ROC measure Aroc ranged 0.55-0.75. Aroc was uncorrelated with accuracy (r = -0.11, P = 0.56). Split-half reliability of Aroc r = 0.69, P = 0.00001. Grey matter in right anterior PFC (BA10) correlated with Aroc (tmax 4.8, P < 0.05 corrected); no link to d' (r = 0.15, P = 0.42) or to confidence level (r = -0.023, P = 0.90).
limits: Small sample for a brain-structure correlation; later large-sample replication of the BA10 link was not checked here. Perceptual task only.
agent_relevance: Confirms that discrimination of confidence is separate from task skill in a clean design. It supports reporting discrimination apart from accuracy for the agent.

source: Rahnev (2024) Measuring metacognition: A comprehensive assessment of current methods
finding: Gap 8 and 6. Large re-analysis of seven Confidence Database datasets, 17 measures, 1,091 subjects (58 excluded, 5.32%). All measures are valid and split-half reliable with over 100 trials. Test-retest reliability is poor. Measures not normalised by d' depend strongly on task difficulty; M-ratio mostly not.
numbers: Split-half r above .837 at 100 trials for all 17 measures, about .965 at 400 (d' is .913 at 100). With 50 trials average r = .424. Test-retest of M-ratio: r = .168 (50 trials), .235 (100), .293 (200), .422 (400); best measure Conf r = .389 to .753; confidence itself above .86. For meta-d', AUC2, gamma, phi, conf: Cohen's d of difficulty effect 2.41, 2.24, 2.64, 1.53, 1.80. M-ratio had a significant difficulty effect in only one of four datasets.
limits: Human perceptual tasks only. Does not itself replicate Maniscalco and Lau (2012) but evaluates the measure they introduced, at scale.
agent_relevance: Single-session M-ratio is noisy even in humans. For the agent, M-ratio needs hundreds of items and fixed difficulty; do not use it as a per-run trust score.

source: Abbasli et al. (2026) Comparing Uncertainty Measurement and Mitigation Methods for LLMs: A Systematic Review (benchmark section)
finding: Gap 10. Post-hoc recalibration (temperature or Platt scaling) helps out of domain for some models only. Platt scaling does better when the held-out set is small.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral-7B-v0.3: partial out-of-domain improvement. Llama 3.1 8B: no significant improvement. Review states the effect is model-dependent and tied to alignment between held-out calibration data and test data.
limits: Open 7-8B models with token-confidence and verbalized baselines, not reasoning models. Does not test the n=250 setting of Luo and Jho.
agent_relevance: A temperature fitted on a small dev set cannot be assumed to carry over; refit per domain and check on held-out domains.

source: Yang et al. (2026) The Mirage of Calibrated Confidence: Trajectory-Independence of Verbalized Confidence in VLMs
finding: Gap 1. In vision-language reasoning models, verbalized confidence barely reacts to what is in the reasoning trace. Confidence given after many self-corrections stays high.
numbers: Eligible hesitation events: confidence before and after the hesitation stayed within 0.02 in 78.5% for Qwen3-VL and 49.0% for VL-Calibration. Calibration training can worsen the disconnect. Proposes a Trajectory-Grounding Score; 10 benchmarks.
limits: Vision-language models, not text agents. Preprint. Only the abstract, method and one result passage were read in detail.
agent_relevance: Reading reasoning before stating confidence does not guarantee confidence is informed by it. Confidence-after-reasoning needs a measured check.

source: Maniscalco and Lau (2012) A signal detection theoretic approach for estimating metacognitive sensitivity from confidence ratings; Koriat (1997) Monitoring one's own knowledge during study
finding: Gap 8, not closed for these two. The ScienceDirect page returned HTTP 403 and Koriat 1997 was not retrievable. I did not read either paper this session. Their content is known only through Rahnev (2024) and Servajean (2026), which use meta-d' as defined in the 2012 paper.
agent_relevance: Keep descriptions of these two sources marked as secondary.
